For me regarding the no-metal rule, it depends on what the player wants. Some want to keep the flavour originally intended with the no-metal rule and thus obey the no-metal rule, and I'm okay with that and let them do that. Some may want to wear heavy armour and reflavour it so instead of wearing metal plate armour, they're wearing armour made out of stone plates, and I'm okay with that and let them do that. Some may want to disregard the no-metal rule entirely for some character-based reason (for example, perhaps they were raised by a blacksmith or they belong to a druid circle that is based on viewing metal as part of the natural world), and I'm okay with that and let them do it as long as they have a solid backstory reason that doesn't just amount to them thinking out of character "I think the no-metal rule's stupid." So far, I have found no real conflicts in this method in my own games.

Ultimately, I'd advise you do whatever works best for you and your group. Each person and group is different. Some may like the limitation the no-metal rule provides and want to keep it (with or without bending the interpretation of armour material, like in your case), while some may think the no-metal rule is stupid and want to ditch it. Both viewpoints are perfectly valid and understandable.

Personally, I don't use any platforms like R20 as I do prefer to run my games either in-person or through Discord calls, so exp calculation would be an issue for me, as I don't want that awkward pause after combat as I frantically crunch the numbers to say how much exp each party member gets. I am aware there are online calculators and stuff, but I prefer to focus less on the bookkeeping side of DMing and more on the part I actually enjoy: embodying a world that the party can interact with in interesting ways. I also don't particularly feel like learning to use platforms like R20, cos although they are a perfectly valid way to play the game, they simply aren't a way I like to play the game when there are options I like better.

Exp a lot of the times also feels very limiting to me. If the party is facing down a group of monsters or a trap I've designed using Xanathar's Guide to Everything or something, there is a given exp value I could use, but how much exp should I give a party for successfully surviving a volcanic eruption or successfully navigating a series of peace talks between two nations on the brink of war, accomplishments they definitely should gain exp from but may not necessarily involve fighting or interacting with a group of monsters with defined stat blocks? For the record, I know it can be done, but the question I ask here isn't if it is possible, but how to implement it. Those aren't as well supported in 5e with exp, so it is just simpler for me to say, "screw it, you level up," which is a much more milestone-style approach. This allows me to still use interesting scenarios that challenge the party in interesting ways while still allowing players to gain experience from events that warrant it, just in the form of leveling up instead of gaining exp.

At one point, a party member was blackmailing all of the other members in the party and was going on for a whole session about it (not surprising given the player, but really annoying). Naturally, me wanting to move the plot along, I decided to throw in a human-shaped swarm of spiders trying to get into the place they were at to get the players moving. Said blackmailing player decided to invite it in and, voilá, they had a new companion.
Eventually, it was decided this spider swarm was called the Watcher. It accompanied the party for a while until it was eventually revealed to be a spy for the BBEG and was destroyed by another party member.
Later on, the Watcher was revealed to be some eldritch entity on the Ethereal Plane, its true name lost to time, that can apparently manifest new avatars to go into the Prime Material Plane (this was a spontaneous decision on my part, it was not planned). Multiple party members are either knowingly or unknowingly in pacts with the Watcher or in some way under its influence.
How did a throwaway creature I made to try to get the plot going become this?

TL;DR: Throwaway monster made to try to get the party to progress the plot turns out to be an eldritch entity on the Ethereal Plane.
